solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In the Bible face behind Benaiah’s last sword

indicators.note: the last of something is its final element, so only the closing letter of the name is kept
one thing sitting behind another fixes the order, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: final letter of the Old Testament warrior's name
Chambers records face meaning wrath in biblical usage, as in the face of the Lord being against evildoers

explanation.surface: A note on scripture: the warrior Benaiah's last weapon, mentioned in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Benaiah really was a biblical swordsman, which makes 'In the Bible' look like scene-setting; it actually qualifies 'face', whose biblical sense is wrath.
explanation.definitionFit: A hanger is a short broadsword formerly carried hanging from a belt, so it is a type of sword.

clue.text: Kept close to mine going up in head-up display

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: egg is old service slang for a mine or bomb
HUD is the standard abbreviation for a head-up display

explanation.surface: A pilot's instrument readout showing that the aircraft hugged a minefield as it climbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is spelled HU-GGE-D: the turned-round egg sits inside the cockpit abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To hug a coast or road is to stay right beside it, so hugged means stayed near to.

clue.text: This troubles restless nag before going in

definitions.note: semi-&lit: the whole clue describes the disease, which afflicts horses

indicators.note: something restless will not stay still, so these letters are moved about
going in means entering, so one piece is put inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Chambers gives an. as an abbreviation of Latin ante, before

explanation.surface: A horse troubled and fidgeting before it goes into its stable.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled horse word supplies the outer NG...A, and the Latin abbreviation for 'before' sits inside it. The whole clue also serves as the definition, since the disease plagues horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagana is a tsetse-borne African disease of cattle and horses, so it does trouble a nag.

clue.text: Low-down Earl contracted nun’s opening book

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information, the low-down
the word cut down to its single-letter abbreviation
a nun is a sister, shortened to sis

explanation.surface: Gossip about a disgraced earl and a nun reading the start of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low-down Earl' reads as a villainous nobleman, but 'Low-down' is a noun meaning information. The 's stands for 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis is the first book of the Bible, the one that opens both the Old Testament and scripture as a whole.

clue.text: Lobby watch as leader departs

indicators.note: when the leader goes, the front letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a sentry keeps watch, standing guard

explanation.surface: Political journalists keep an eye on things as their chief walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lobby' suggests political lobbying or lobby journalists, but here it is the room by a front door.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is a passage or hall just inside an entrance, the same space a lobby occupies.

clue.text: Fly round current ship being lightly touched

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses others

blocks.note: a ked is a parasitic fly, the sheep ked
I is the symbol for electric current
SS, steamship, is the usual prefix for a ship

explanation.surface: An insect circles a vessel moving with the current until it barely brushes it.
explanation.walkthrough: The obscure fly KED is a Mephisto favourite; it opens up to hold the electrical symbol and the steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss can mean a light glancing contact, as when a ball kisses another in snooker.

clue.text: It’s impossible to get into this shape, sadly not like belt

definitions.text: It’s impossible to get into this shape

indicators.note: something sadly done is done badly, so the following letters end up disordered

blocks.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint about failing to squeeze into some outfit that fits nothing like a belt.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a dieter's lament, but it is mathematical: this surface cannot exist in ordinary three-dimensional space without passing through itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A Klein bottle is a closed one-sided surface whose inside is its outside, so nothing can truly be put into it.

clue.text: Lacking finish clue is “Ploughed furrows”

indicators.note: without its finish, the final letter of the word goes
ploughed ground is turned over, so these letters are churned into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword setter admits an unfinished hint is just a description of a ploughed field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ploughed furrows' looks like one phrase, but 'Ploughed' is the anagram signal and 'furrows' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sulci is the Latin plural of sulcus, an anatomical term for a groove, especially on the brain's surface.

clue.text: Question in saying starts to kick start loud complaints

indicators.note: to be in something is to be held inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: a saw is an old saying or proverb
QU is the standard abbreviation for question
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone asks why kick-starting a motorbike provokes such noisy grumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kick start' looks like the motorbike action, but it supplies two initial letters. SAW is an old word for a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A squawk is a harsh cry, and by extension a loud protest or grievance.

clue.text: Poets like Gray, for example, in English borders

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a list is a border or edging strip, as on cloth
the usual abbreviation, exempli gratia

explanation.surface: A note that poets such as Thomas Gray turn up along the English borders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English borders' tempts a solver to put E at both ends, but E is just English and 'borders' is the word LISTS. Thomas Gray wrote the famous Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of elegies, mournful reflective poems, are elegists, and Gray's Elegy makes him the classic example.

clue.text: Prepare to accept universal pressure

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece receives the other

blocks.note: to dress food or a wound is to prepare it
U is the film-classification abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: Advice to brace yourself for pressure that everyone faces.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is coercion or constraint by threats, a forceful kind of pressure.

clue.text: Desperately well-bred bloke in commotion wasting hour

indicators.note: wasting something means losing it, so a letter is thrown away
to be in something is to be held inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: hurly is a commotion, as in hurly-burly
H is the abbreviation for hour, here the letter removed
a gent, short for gentleman, is a well-bred man

explanation.surface: A gentleman caught up in a fuss frantically loses an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desperately' could be an anagram signal, but it is the definition; hurly is the first half of hurly-burly, an old word for uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting desperately means acting with pressing need, which is what urgently describes.

clue.text: Regius professor is on god’s “blood” amid support for Muse

indicators.note: one thing on another follows it here, fixing the order
amid means in the middle of, so these pieces sit inside another

blocks.note: a tee supports a golf ball
RP for Regius Professor, with 's standing for is
ichor is the fluid said to flow in the veins of Greek gods

explanation.surface: A senior academic, steeped in mythology, lectures on divine blood while backing a Muse.
explanation.walkthrough: A Regius Professor holds a royally founded chair at a British university, abbreviated RP. The golf tee splits round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Terpsichore is one of the nine Muses of Greek myth, presiding over dance and choral song.

clue.text: Recipient’s suit in US, full of slang-whang

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so one piece contains the other

blocks.note: Chambers gives gee as an American verb meaning to suit or fit together
slang-whang is noisy ranting talk

explanation.surface: A lawsuit in America brought by someone full of bluster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' looks like a lawsuit, but it is a verb, matching the American sense of gee.
explanation.definitionFit: A grantee is the person to whom a grant is made, so the one receiving it.

clue.text: Who’d bond with one going downhill fast? Good going first

indicators.note: going first means moving to the front, so this letter leaves its place and leads

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, which moves
a luger rides a luge, a racing toboggan, minus its G here

explanation.surface: Who would make friends with a speed skier? Being good comes first.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the G out of LUGER and put it at the front. 'bond' hints at friendship but means stick together.
explanation.definitionFit: One who glues things sticks them together, which is what bonding means in the adhesive sense.

clue.text: Just after entering Germany I’m done for

definitions.note: a phrase a goner might say, standing in for the noun

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: GER is an abbreviation for Germany
on can mean immediately after, as in on arrival

explanation.surface: Someone who has just arrived in Germany despairs that it is all over for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cry rather than a noun: whoever says 'I'm done for' is a goner.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is a person beyond help or doomed, exactly the state of someone declaring their ruin.

clue.text: Wife with carer’s allowance, for example, backing case of the heart?

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: Eve was made from Adam's rib, so a wife is jocularly a rib
initials of the UK benefit Carer's Allowance
the usual abbreviation, turned round

explanation.surface: A wife claiming a state benefit, and backing a sentimental case.
explanation.walkthrough: Carer's Allowance is a British welfare payment for people looking after someone. 'case of the heart' sounds like romance; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The rib cage is the bony enclosure protecting the heart and lungs, so it literally encases the heart.

clue.text: What zebra does concerning mate on eastern edge of Serengeti

indicators.note: an edge is a border, so only an outer letter of the word is kept, here the first

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
fere is an old word for a companion or mate
standard abbreviation
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A wildlife note on how a zebra behaves with its mate in the eastern Serengeti.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zebra' and 'Serengeti' set an African scene, but zebra is American slang for a referee, after the striped shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports official in a black-and-white striped shirt is nicknamed a zebra, and what such an official does is officiate games.

clue.text: Ground staff relieving American social group of article

indicators.note: relieving someone of a thing takes it away, so letters are removed

blocks.note: Kiwanis is an American service club
an is the indefinite article, removed

explanation.surface: Airport workers relieving a US club of some item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground staff' is not airport staff in the usual sense: kiwis are RAF slang for non-flying personnel, after the flightless bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Like the flightless New Zealand bird, air force kiwis never fly and stay on the airfield.

clue.text: Cards could be passed over with small orders

indicators.note: something passed over is flipped across, so the letters go the other way

blocks.note: to live is to be, to exist
standard abbreviation
to book is to order a place or ticket

explanation.surface: Some playing cards might be overlooked when small orders are filled.
explanation.walkthrough: The puritan name for playing cards is the devil's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing cards were condemned by moralists as the devil's books, a nickname for a pack used in gambling.

clue.text: Capacity to combine farewell with start of cruise in New York

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept
to be in something is to be inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: vale is Latin for farewell
standard abbreviation
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A liner's ability to mix a goodbye party with the start of a cruise from New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capacity to combine' sounds like multitasking but is a chemistry term.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry valency measures how many bonds an atom can form with others.

clue.text: Biblical bush? Wind about to avoid it with endless smoke

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped
without an end, the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: to wind is to coil
c. for circa, about, which is removed
't, the clipped form of it
reek is Scots for smoke, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A wind blows round a smoking bush, as in the burning bush of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The burning bush of Exodus is the trap; this plant is named in Isaiah. The question mark admits a tree is called a bush.
explanation.definitionFit: The oil tree appears in Isaiah 41:19 among trees planted in the wilderness, so it is a scriptural plant.

clue.text: In poems strike adjective (they did it in Latin), standard raised

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising means lifting upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: a. is the abbreviation for adjective
ff. stands for fecerunt, Latin for they made it, as on artworks
par is a standard or norm

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on old verse, with a Latin aside and standards raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In poems' marks a Spenserian word. Fecerunt is the plural of fecit, the signature on old engravings.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser used affrap to mean strike or hit, so it is a poetic verb for a blow.

clue.text: I’m in twig near trees, very exclusive

indicators.note: excluding very means leaving out its abbreviation, so one letter is removed

blocks.note: Chambers gives twig as an old word for fashion or style
a vista can be an avenue or row of trees, minus the V for very

explanation.surface: Someone who has climbed in among twigs near the trees calls it a very select spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twig near trees' reads as a forest; the definition is the whole boast 'I'm in', meaning fashionable. 'near' just places one piece next to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashionista lives for being in style, and saying you are in means you are trendy.

clue.text: A daughter learned to be anxious no more

definitions.note: 'no more' marks the word as obsolete

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation
someone well read is learned

explanation.surface: A daughter discovers that she need not worry any longer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anxious no more' looks like relief, but 'no more' signals an obsolete word: this one is archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Adread is an old word for afraid or in dread, the archaic equivalent of fearful.

clue.text: Lines in eccentric rim

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is held by the other

blocks.note: fey can mean whimsical or odd
L for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Markings around an off-centre wheel edge, as in engineering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric rim' suggests a mechanical eccentric, but 'eccentric' is the odd FEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A felly, also felloe, is the outer wooden ring of a spoked wheel.

clue.text: Nothing up with air-conditioned scientific apparatus

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: nil means nothing
AC is the abbreviation for air conditioning

explanation.surface: A laboratory complaint that nothing works with the air conditioning on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing up' reads as 'nothing wrong', but 'up' turns the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Linac is short for linear accelerator, a physics machine that speeds up particles.

clue.text: Lotus’s bounce upset parent

indicators.note: something upset is turned over, so in a down clue the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: to dap is to bounce, as a ball does
ma is a mother

explanation.surface: A Lotus sports car jolts and annoys a passenger's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lotus' evokes the British car maker, but it is the flower. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Padma is the Sanskrit name for the sacred lotus flower of Hindu and Buddhist imagery.

clue.text: Bikini maybe is for everything outside

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: to and for are interchangeable in phrases like a key for the door
all means everything

explanation.surface: A swimsuit described as suitable for everyone, worn outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bikini' looks like swimwear, but it is the Pacific atoll used for nuclear tests; 'maybe' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands is a ring-shaped coral reef island, an example of the answer.

clue.text: Let out inmate finally in panic

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter, which alone is kept
to be in something is to be held inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a fright is a sudden panic
its final letter

explanation.surface: A prisoner is released at last, amid general alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let out' looks like releasing a prisoner, but Chambers gives freight as a verb meaning to hire out a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To freight a vessel can mean to let it out on hire for carrying cargo, the leasing sense of let.

clue.text: Oil from communion table when Latin is what closes Eucharist

indicators.note: what closes a word is its final letter, which is the one taken
saying one thing is where another was means it stands in that place, a swap

blocks.note: the altar is the communion table in church
its final letter, replacing the L for Latin

explanation.surface: Holy oil taken from the altar during a Latin Mass at the end of the Eucharist.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the abbreviation for Latin; swap it in the church table for the last letter of the sacrament.
explanation.definitionFit: Attar is a fragrant essential oil distilled from flowers, especially rose petals.

clue.text: Fathom out Spenser’s stranger is to go quickly in his poem

definitions.text: to go quickly in his poem

indicators.note: something out is gone, so this letter is dropped

blocks.note: frenne is Spenser's word for a stranger or foreigner
F is the abbreviation for fathom, removed

explanation.surface: A reader trying to work out Spenser's stranger, who rushes through his epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fathom out' looks like 'work out'; it is the measure F, removed. Both words are from Spenser's Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Renne is Spenser's archaic spelling of run, the verb for moving fast on foot.

clue.text: On Lady Day, see one abandoning foul pink

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so these letters are dropped

blocks.note: o' is the clipped form of on
LD is the abbreviation for Lady Day, 25 March
virose means poisonous or foul-smelling
V for vide, see, and I for one, both removed

explanation.surface: On a March feast day, someone spots a person leaving behind an ugly pink.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Day is the Feast of the Annunciation on 25 March, once a British quarter day. Take V and I from the front of VIROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Old rose is a dusty greyish-pink colour, so it names a shade of pink.

clue.text: Fungi marks in timber fully returned

definitions.note: plural, while the answer names a single genus of fungi

indicators.note: to be in something is to be inside it, so one piece is placed within another
something returned comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a tree is a source of timber
M for marks, the former German currency
all can mean wholly or fully

explanation.surface: Fungus leaves marks on wood that has been completely sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marks in timber' reads as stains, but the marks are the currency abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tremella is a genus of jelly fungi that grows on dead wood, so it names a group of fungi.

clue.text: Quietly and, yes, movingly capturing chaplain’s soul

indicators.note: moving letters about changes their order, so they are rearranged
to capture is to take in and hold, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: p for piano, quietly
taken as written, to be rearranged
CH is an abbreviation for chaplain

explanation.surface: A chaplain's soul captured quietly and movingly, with a soft yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movingly' looks like emotional praise, but it signals the rearrangement of the agreeing word around the chaplain.
explanation.definitionFit: Psyche is the Greek word for the soul or mind, used in English for a person's spirit.

clue.text: Priest captivated by extravagantly exuberant nymph

indicators.note: someone captivated is held captive, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: mad can mean wildly excited or extravagantly enthusiastic
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel, a crossword stock priest

explanation.surface: A cleric falls under the spell of a wildly lively nymph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivated' sounds romantic, but it just means held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a maelid is a nymph of apple trees, one of the minor nature spirits.
